text:
In late August 1854, cholera struck Soho, a crowded, poor district of London. Within about ten days, more than five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of one another were dead. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhoea and rapid dehydration. In the worst cases, a healthy person could be dead within a day. Nobody knew what caused it.

The prevailing belief was the miasma theory: disease spread through "bad air", foul-smelling vapours rising from rotting waste, swamps and sewers. It was a reasonable idea in a city that stank. London's streets were thick with sewage, and the Thames itself was an open drain. The idea of germs, living organisms too small to see that could cause illness, had not yet been accepted. Louis Pasteur's work was still years away.

John Snow, a physician who lived a short walk from the outbreak, was unconvinced by miasma. He had been thinking about cholera for years. He had noticed that the illness struck the gut first, not the lungs, which made no sense if people were simply breathing something poisonous. He suspected instead that the disease passed from person to person through something swallowed, most likely water contaminated by the waste of the sick. In 1849 he had published this idea, and it had been largely ignored. Snow was well respected for his pioneering work on anaesthesia, but he was not a man the establishment felt obliged to follow on this question.

The Soho outbreak gave him a chance to test his theory. He did something ordinary and powerful: he went door to door and asked questions. Where had the dead lived? Where did they get their water? Snow collected the addresses of victims from the local register of deaths, and he began plotting them on a map of the neighbourhood, marking each death with a bar. The pattern that emerged was striking. The deaths clustered tightly around a public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew their drinking water by hand.

Clustering alone was not proof, so Snow looked harder at the exceptions, which turned out to be the most persuasive evidence. A workhouse near the pump, housing hundreds of people, had very few deaths. Snow learned it had its own well on the premises, so its inmates did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street had almost no cases either. The workers there were given free beer and, it seems, drank little water, and the brewery too had its own supply.

Then came the opposite kind of exception. A woman who lived far away in Hampstead died of cholera. Snow discovered that she had once lived near Broad Street and so liked the taste of the water that she had it delivered to her, in a large container, every day. Her niece, who drank it too, also died. No one else in their neighbourhood fell ill. Snow considered this a nearly perfect natural experiment: miasma could not explain a death so far from the supposed source of bad air, but contaminated water could.

On 7 September, Snow took his evidence to the Board of Guardians of St James's parish, the local authority. He urged them to act. They were sceptical, but they agreed to a modest step and removed the handle from the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already waning by then, and many people had fled the area, so it is hard to say how much the handle's removal mattered. Snow himself was careful on this point. Even so, the removal became the most famous gesture in the history of public health.

Snow's investigation did not end there. A local clergyman, the Reverend Henry Whitehead, began as a sceptic of Snow's theory and set out to prove it wrong. Instead, his own careful enquiries among his parishioners strengthened Snow's case. Whitehead went on to identify what was probably the origin of the outbreak. A baby in a house on Broad Street had died of cholera just before the epidemic began, and her mother had washed the child's soiled nappies and emptied the water into a cesspool. That cesspool was found to be leaking, and it lay only a few feet from the pump's well. A later inspection showed that the well's brickwork was in poor condition, allowing waste to seep in.

Even so, the official response was lukewarm. A committee investigating the outbreak concluded that it saw no reason to accept Snow's theory, and the miasma view continued to dominate. Snow died in 1858, at only forty-five, without seeing his ideas widely accepted. Not long afterwards, an enormous stench in the summer of 1858, known as the Great Stink, spurred London to build a modern sewer system, an irony given that the authorities did so partly out of fear of bad air.

Over the following decades, the germ theory of disease took hold, and Snow's work was recognised as a founding achievement of epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His map and his careful reasoning, comparing those who fell ill with those who did not, remain a model of how to find a cause from patterns in the evidence.
